PASSO 1: as cores principais são: rojo,: STEP 1: the main colors are: rojo, azul, verde, amarillo, negro, blanco, gris, marrón, naranja and rosa. Say each one out loud, minding the sounds: «amarillo» sounds like «ah-mah-REE-lyo», and «azul» starts with the Castilian «th» sound (ah-THOOL). STEP 2: a color is an adjective and goes AFTER the noun: «una camisa blanca», «unos zapatos negros». You can't say «una blanca camisa». STEP 3: colors ending in «-o» have four forms: «rojo, roja, rojos, rojas». STEP 4: colors ending in «-e» or a consonant have only two: singular and plural. «Verde / verdes», «azul / azules» (the «z» becomes «c» before «-es»), «gris / grises», «marrón / marrones». STEP 5: «naranja» and «rosa» use the same form for masculine and feminine: «un abrigo naranja», «una falda rosa». STEP 6: to lighten or darken a color, add «claro» or «oscuro» to it, without changing the color word itself: «una camisa azul claro» (light blue), «un abrigo verde oscuro» (dark green). STEP 7: «pantalones» is plural: «unos pantalones», and the adjective agrees: «unos pantalones negros». You say «un pantalón» for a single piece. In Spain, «los vaqueros» are jeans; in Latin America you'll hear «los jeans». STEP 8: pronunciation: the «ll» in «amarillo» and «zapatillas» sounds like an English «y» in Spain; the «ch» in «chaqueta» sounds like English «ch»; the «z» in «zapatos» sounds like the Castilian «th».
em português o adjetivo também concorda: English colors also come after the noun when functioning as a true predicate, but as a modifier they normally come BEFORE it: «a white shirt», «black shoes» — exactly the mirror image of Spanish word order, where the color always trails the noun. English colors also never change their ending for gender or number («white shirt», «white shirts», whether the noun is masculine or feminine in another language), so the four-way or two-way agreement pattern here (rojo/roja/rojos/rojas) is new ground to learn.
The color agrees in gender with «camisa».

Perguntar o preço, provar e pagar: Asking the price, trying things on, and paying
PASSO 1: para perguntar o preço de uma p: STEP 1: to ask the price of one item, say «¿Cuánto cuesta?»; for several, «¿Cuánto cuestan?». «Costar» changes o → ue (cuesta, cuestan). For the total, «¿Cuánto es?». STEP 2: to ask for something, use «Quisiera…», «Busco…» or «¿Tiene…?»: «Busco una chaqueta negra» (I'm looking for a black jacket), «¿Tiene esto en una talla más grande?» (do you have this in a bigger size? — the word «más» is covered in lesson 26; for now just use the set phrase). With «tú», «¿Tienes…?». STEP 3: to try something on: «¿Puedo probarme esta camisa?» («probarse» changes o → ue: me pruebo). STEP 4: to say how it fits, use these set phrases: «Me queda bien» (it fits me well), «Me queda grande» (it's too big on me), «Me queda pequeño» (it's too small on me). STEP 5: to pay: «¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?» (can I pay by card?), «Pago en efectivo» (I'll pay cash). Note: «con tarjeta» (by card) and «en efectivo» (in cash). STEP 6: numbers 100 to 1000: cien, ciento uno, ciento dos… doscientos, trescientos, cuatrocientos, quinientos, seiscientos, setecientos, ochocientos, novecientos, mil. Exact hundred: «cien euros». With one more unit: «ciento cinco». STEP 7: the hundreds agree with the noun: «doscientos euros», but «doscientas camisas». STEP 8: prices: «9,50 €» is read as «nueve euros con cincuenta». In writing, Spain uses a comma for the cents. In other countries the currency and the way prices are read change: pesos, dollars, soles. STEP 9: pronunciation: «quinientos» sounds like kee-NYEN-tos; «cien» sounds like thyen; «ciento» sounds like THYEN-to.
em português dizemos «quanto custa?» e «: English «how much does it cost?» and «how much do they cost?» follow the same singular/plural logic Spanish does, so that part transfers directly. The round-hundred words are where the real difference shows up: English just says «five hundred, seven hundred, nine hundred» with no irregularity at all, while Spanish «quinientos» (not «cincocientos»), «setecientos» (not «sietecientos») and «novecientos» (not «nuevecientos») change shape in ways you simply have to memorize. And «cien» shifting to «ciento» the moment something follows it («ciento veinte») has no parallel in English «one hundred» at all.

Os demonstrativos: este, ese e aquel: The demonstratives: este, ese, and aquel
PASSO 1: os demonstrativos mostram algo: STEP 1: demonstratives point at something and signal distance. «Este» is for what's near the speaker; «ese» is for what's near the listener or a bit further away; «aquel» is for what's far from both. They pair with «aquí, ahí, allí». STEP 2: the forms of «este»: este, esta, estos, estas. Of «ese»: ese, esa, esos, esas. Of «aquel»: aquel, aquella, aquellos, aquellas. STEP 3: the demonstrative agrees with the noun in gender and number and comes before it: «esta camisa», «ese abrigo», «aquellos zapatos». STEP 4: without the noun, the demonstrative works as a pronoun: «Quiero este» (I want this one), «¿Cuánto cuesta esa?» (how much does that one cost?). Today it's written with no accent mark. STEP 5: «esto», «eso» and «aquello» are neuter: they're for an unidentified thing or an idea, and they never change form: «¿Qué es esto?» (what's this?), «Eso es caro» (that's expensive). STEP 6: there's no fusion with a preposition: «in this» is «en este», «of/from this» is «de esta», «in that» is «en ese». STEP 7: to choose between two things: «¿Cuál prefieres: este o ese?» (which do you prefer, this one or that one?) — lesson 16 covers more of this.
o português tem a mesma divisão em três:: English also has this near/far distinction, but collapses it into just two words, «this» and «that», where Spanish keeps three levels of distance (este/ese/aquel) tied to speaker, listener, and neither. And where English happily fuses a preposition straight onto the demonstrative-adjacent phrase («in this store»), Spanish never fuses the preposition onto the demonstrative itself: it's always «en esta tienda», never a contracted form, and «of that coat» is «de ese abrigo», word for word, with no shortcut.
Those shoes over there are cheap.
«Pantalones» is plural, and so is the verb.
